After a Car or Truck Crash in Washington: What the First Thirty Days Decide

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·November 11, 2026

A pickup came through the stop sign on Sprague and caught your driver's door. The officer took names and left, your car went to a tow yard in Spokane Valley, and two days later the other driver's insurer called to ask whether you would mind giving a short recorded statement. Your neck is stiff and you have not seen a doctor yet because it did not seem bad enough. Nothing in those first weeks feels like a legal event, but most of what later decides the claim is fixed during them, by what gets reported, what gets said, and what gets written down.

What does Washington law require of me at the scene?

RCW 46.52.020 sets the duties. A driver involved in a crash that injures or kills anyone must stop at or as near the scene as possible and stay until the information exchange is done. Every driver in a crash involving injury, an attended vehicle, or other property must give a name, address, insurance company, policy number and license plate number, must show a driver's license, and must give reasonable assistance to anyone injured, including arranging transport to a doctor or hospital when treatment is plainly needed or the injured person asks for it.

Two provisions answer the usual hesitation. Under RCW 46.52.020(3), helping an injured person or otherwise complying is not evidence that you were the one at fault. And in a crash with only vehicle or property damage, RCW 46.52.020(2)(a) requires the cars to be moved off the main lanes as soon as possible and says that moving them in no way affects fault. Leaving an injury crash without doing these things is a class C felony under RCW 46.52.020(4)(b).

Do I have to file a collision report in Washington?

Sometimes. RCW 46.52.030(1) requires the driver of any vehicle involved in a crash resulting in injury, death, or damage to the property of any one person at or above the reporting threshold to make a written report within four days. The report goes to the police chief if the crash happened inside a city or town, and to the county sheriff or the State Patrol if it happened outside one. The duty does not apply when a law enforcement officer is making the report under RCW 46.52.030(3).

The statute leaves the dollar figure to the State Patrol. RCW 46.52.030(5) set it at five hundred dollars in 1987 and allows it to be adjusted for inflation by rule, and WAC 446-85-010 has set it at one thousand dollars since January 1, 2015. An injury takes the dollar question off the table entirely.

If an officer came, get the report or incident number before leaving. If none came, the four days run while you are still dealing with a tow yard and a rental. The driver's report is protected. RCW 46.52.080 makes a required report "without prejudice to the individual so reporting" and provides that, apart from narrow exceptions, it may not be used as evidence in a civil or criminal trial arising out of the crash, while still requiring the names, plates, and the date, time and place to be disclosed to people with a proper interest, including the drivers, anyone injured, and their attorneys and insurers.

The other driver's insurance company called. What should I tell them?

Their adjuster works for the person who hit you. You have no policy with that company obliging you to give it a recorded statement, and the first weeks are the worst time to give one, because you do not yet know what is wrong with you. A statement that your neck was "a little sore" on day three is a sentence that will be read back to you after the MRI.

What is reasonable to give them is narrow: your name and how to reach you, the claim number, where the car is so it can be inspected, and the fact that you were hurt and are being treated. A blanket medical authorization does not need to be signed this early.

The claims rules in chapter 284-30 WAC put some limits on how the other side's insurer may deal with you. WAC 284-30-380(6) bars an insurer from suggesting that a third-party claimant's rights may be impaired if a form or release is not completed within a specified time, except to give notice of a statute of limitations. If it keeps negotiating directly with you while you have no lawyer, WAC 284-30-380(5) requires it to give you written notice sixty days before a limitation period may expire. And once you have a lawyer, WAC 284-30-330(19) bars the insurer from negotiating or settling directly with you without the lawyer's knowledge and consent. Your own insurer is a different relationship with different duties, which the companion article on PIP and underinsured motorist claims covers.

If this is describing your situation, tell me what is going on. I read what comes in myself, and I will tell you whether it is something I can help with.

Tell me about your situation

Who pays my medical bills right after a crash?

Usually your own policy, through personal injury protection, if you carry it. For your injuries, the other driver's insurer ordinarily pays once, at the end, in exchange for a release. PIP fills the gap, and RCW 48.22.085(1) requires it to be offered on every automobile liability policy issued or renewed in Washington.

Three details matter in the first month. Medical and hospital benefits under RCW 48.22.005(7) cover reasonable and necessary expenses incurred within three years of the crash, so there is no reason to delay treatment waiting for fault to be sorted out. Income continuation benefits under RCW 48.22.005(3) begin fourteen days after the crash, which is when the first missed paycheck tends to hurt. And PIP is limited to the actual amount of loss or expense under RCW 48.22.005(12), so the bills and wage records are what drive it.

Open the PIP claim early and tell every provider that the treatment is crash related. Whether you have PIP at all is on your declarations page, and RCW 48.22.085(2) makes a written rejection by a named insured binding on everyone the coverage would otherwise have reached.

What if the police say I was partly at fault?

The report is not the verdict, and in Washington a share of fault is not the end of the claim. RCW 4.22.005 provides that the claimant's contributory fault "diminishes proportionately" the damages awarded, "but does not bar recovery." Twenty percent at fault means a smaller recovery, not no recovery.

The first month is when the fault picture can still move: photographs of where the vehicles stopped, witnesses the officer missed, and any camera facing the intersection, whose video is often overwritten within days.

The same chapter reaches what you do after the crash. RCW 4.22.015 defines fault to include an "unreasonable failure to avoid an injury or to mitigate damages." Skipping the follow-up appointment, stopping physical therapy, or waiting six weeks to see anyone are the facts an insurer uses to argue that some of the harm is yours.

Who is liable in a commercial truck crash besides the driver?

A truck crash often has more than one company behind it. RCW 46.32.005 defines a commercial motor vehicle to include one with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,001 pounds or more used in commerce, and the tractor, the trailer, the load and the driver can each belong to different businesses.

Washington's fault statute is built for that. RCW 4.22.070(1) has the trier of fact assign a percentage of fault to every entity that caused the damages, and RCW 4.22.070(1)(a) makes a party responsible for the fault of another person where that person "was acting as an agent or servant of the party." Whether a particular driver was acting for a particular company is a factual question, and so is whether a loader, a maintenance shop, or a broker added fault of its own.

The records exist because the industry is regulated. RCW 46.32.020 authorizes the State Patrol to adopt rules on vehicle inspections, drivers' qualifications and hours of service, and directs it to prioritize higher-risk motor carriers for inspections and compliance reviews. A preservation letter to the carrier in the first weeks, asking it to keep the driver's logs, electronic data, inspection and maintenance records and dispatch communications, is the step that puts the carrier on notice to keep them.

How long do I have, and what if a government vehicle hit me?

Three years in the ordinary case. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for "any other injury to the person or rights of another," which covers a car or truck crash.

A crash with a city bus, a county truck, a school bus or a State Patrol car adds a step in front of that. A tort claim has to be presented first, and no lawsuit can be filed until sixty calendar days after it is presented, under RCW 4.96.020(4) for local government and RCW 4.92.110 for the state. The limitation period is tolled during the sixty days. The companion article on tort claims against government entities covers how to present one.

One more number belongs in the first month. RCW 46.30.020 requires drivers to carry liability insurance, or another listed form of financial responsibility, of at least the amounts in RCW 46.29.090: twenty-five thousand dollars for injury to one person and fifty thousand for two or more in one accident. That is often all the other side has, which is why your own underinsured motorist coverage should be identified now.

Where this goes wrong

The recorded statement given in week one, before a diagnosis, to an adjuster whose job is to close the file.

No report and no report number. The crash was over the threshold, nobody filed within four days, and later nobody can find the other driver's insurer.

Treatment starts late, or stops when the PIP adjuster first questions a bill. Under RCW 4.22.015 that gap becomes an argument about fault, not only about damages.

The truck is back on the road and its data and logs are overwritten, because nobody sent a preservation letter.

A crash with a government vehicle is handled like any other, and the tort claim is never presented or is presented to the wrong office.

The property damage check comes with a release nobody reads for whether it covers more than the car.

What a lawyer does here

Most of the early work is preservation and paperwork. Getting the report and the video before they are gone. Sending preservation letters to every company behind a commercial vehicle. Opening the PIP claim and finding the underinsured motorist coverage on every policy in the household. Taking the adjuster's calls so nothing said on day three becomes the measure of your injury. Calendaring the three years and, where a public entity is involved, the claim and the sixty days. And giving you an honest read on comparative fault while the evidence that moves it can still be gathered.

I handle car and truck accident claims from my office in downtown Spokane, and I represent clients throughout Washington. I am admitted in Washington, WSBA #55307, and Oregon, OSB #242384.

If you were hurt in a crash, I offer a free consultation by appointment at my Spokane office, 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400. Bring the report or incident number, the declarations page for your own auto policy, photographs, and anything the other driver's insurer has sent you.
